summary: Defines MIB objects for managing RIP version 2 with SNMP. It is a standards-track document that gives network management tools a standard view of RIP-2 routers.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of gauges to check how a router's route-sharing is doing.

questions: what is the rip version 2 mib
how to manage rip with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring RIP version 2: counters, per-interface settings and a peer table.

tldr.problem: Operators needed a standard SNMP view of RIP version 2 routers, and the earlier RIP-2 MIB in RFC 1389 did not cover unnumbered interfaces and still encoded the Routing Domain concept.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the RIPv2-MIB module with global counters, two per-interface tables (status and configuration) and an optional peer table. It deprecates Routing Domain and adds unnumbered interfaces, Demand RIP send modes and MD5 authentication.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 1389 and gives network management tools a common way to read and set RIP-2 behavior.

today: RFC 1724 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1389. The Draft Standard status and the obsoleted RFC come from the RFC's own metadata; the text records no later developments.

sections.title: What the Memo Defines
sections.content:
RFC 1724 defines the part of the Management Information Base (MIB) used to manage RIP Version 2. It obsoletes RFC 1389. The module is called RIPv2-MIB and sits at mib-2 23.

It builds on the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: the SMI (RFC 1155), the concise description format (RFC 1212), MIB-II (RFC 1213) and SNMP (RFC 1157). Objects are named by object identifiers and described with a restricted subset of ASN.1.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook that lets any manager's tool read the gauges on a router that shares routes using RIP version 2.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The module has three kinds of content. Global counters help spot the effects of RIP incompatibilities. Two interface tables hold per-interface statistics and per-interface configuration. An optional peer table helps debug neighbor relationships.

The global counters are rip2GlobalRouteChanges, the number of route changes RIP made to the IP route database (not counting a refresh of a route's age), and rip2GlobalQueries, the number of responses sent to RIP queries from other systems. The interface and global groups are mandatory for systems that implement RIP-2. The peer group is optional in the group comments, though the compliance statement lists it as a mandatory group.

One new data type is defined, RouteTag, a 2-octet string that holds the Route Domain field of a packet header or route entry.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges come in three sets: a few overall counters, a panel for each network port, and a list of neighbor routers.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1389
sections.content:
Route Domains are deprecated in the protocol, so they are deprecated in the MIB. rip2IfConfDomain is marked obsolete, and rip2PeerDomain, which cannot be removed because it is an index, must always be zero.

Unnumbered interfaces are now supported. Since the neighbor's address may be unknown, a pseudo-address in network 0.0.0.0 is used, where the low 24 bits are the ifIndex of the IP interface. The new rip2IfConfSrcAddress object sets the source address on an unnumbered interface.

rip2IfConfSend gains two values for Demand RIP under RIP-I and RIP-II rules, which avoids needing a separate Demand RIP MIB. MD5 authentication is also supported.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rulebook drops an old feature nobody uses, and adds support for ports with no address, a mode for phone-line style links, and a stronger password check.

sections.title: Interface Status and Configuration
sections.content:
Both interface tables are indexed by the interface's IP address. The status table counts bad RIP response packets received, bad routes ignored in valid packets, and triggered updates sent. Full updates carrying new information are explicitly not counted as triggered updates.

The configuration table sets how the router behaves on each interface. rip2IfConfSend chooses what is sent, with a default of rip1Compatible. rip2IfConfReceive chooses which version is accepted, with a default of rip1OrRip2. rip2IfConfDefaultMetric ranges from 0 to 15, and 0 means no default route is originated, although a default route via another router may still be propagated. Rows are removed by writing invalid to the row status.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network port has a counting panel and a settings panel. The settings decide which kind of route-sharing messages the port sends and accepts.

sections.title: Authentication and the Peer Table
sections.content:
rip2IfConfAuthType selects noAuthentication (the default), simplePassword or md5. The key in rip2IfConfAuthKey is up to 16 octets; a shorter key is left-justified and padded on the right with nulls. Reading the key always returns a zero-length string, so authentication cannot be bypassed by reading the MIB.

The optional peer table describes active peers, meaning routers from which a valid RIP update was heard in the last 180 seconds. For each peer it gives the address used as source, the time of the last update, the RIP version in the last packet, and counts of bad packets and bad routes.
sections.plainLanguage: The password for a port can be set but never read back, so nobody can peek at it. A separate list shows which neighbor routers spoke up recently.

sections.title: Conformance and Security
sections.content:
The compliance statement lists four mandatory groups: global, interface status, interface configuration and peer. Each group is a plain list of the objects described above.

The Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that claims to support this must offer all four sets of gauges.

items.label: ripVersion1
items.desc: Send RIP updates compliant with RFC 1058.

items.label: rip1Compatible
items.desc: Broadcast RIP-2 updates using RFC 1058 route subsumption rules.

items.desc: Demand RIP on a WAN interface under RIP Version 1 rules.

items.desc: Demand RIP on a WAN interface under Version 2 rules.
